verdict.difficultyReason: Credentials are available on a normal account with no required review.
verdict.useCase: an agent that acts on behalf of a user's GitHub account (reads repos, issues and PRs) through the builder's own OAuth app, including access to users' organization resources

timeToCredentials.basis: Our estimate: registration is a single settings form on a signed-in account (s6) with no review step described, so minutes to a couple of hours including verifying an email address.

humanEffortHours.basis: Our estimate: registration is short, but implementing the auth flow, token handling and per-organization approval requests take developer time and coordination with org owners.

verdict.summary: Registering your own GitHub OAuth app is a quick, account-only job with no GitHub review in the sources. The real hurdle is organizations: those with OAuth app access restrictions must have an owner approve your app before it can reach their private resources.
verdict.biggestLaunchRisk: Organizations with OAuth app access restrictions (on by default for new orgs) block unapproved OAuth apps from private org resources until an org owner approves them.

managedCovers.text: Composio's managed-auth directory lists GitHub as having Composio-managed OAuth available, so a shared OAuth app may be usable for prototyping without registering your own.

youNeedOwnWhen.text: You want your own app's name, Client ID and callback URL shown to users on the GitHub authorization page. The sources do not say what the managed app displays.

Organization owners need to approve a specific OAuth app under access restrictions. Approval applies to the OAuth app in question, so whose app it is matters (the sources do not say how this works for a shared managed app).
You need control over token settings such as expiring tokens, or your own rate-limit budget and app-level settings.

requirements.text: A GitHub account that can open the OAuth app registration page in settings.
A verified email address on the account of any user who authorizes the app.
An Authorization callback URL that you own and control, since ownership of it prevents token leakage to an attacker.

For org resources: an owner of each restricted organization must approve the app.

steps.title: Decide between an OAuth app and a GitHub App
steps.detail: GitHub recommends considering a GitHub App instead (fine-grained permissions, short-lived tokens, higher scaling rate limits). This guide covers the OAuth app route you asked for.
steps.agentPrep: Summarize the OAuth app vs GitHub App differences for the team.

evidence.label: tested
evidence.testNote: Only reachability was observed: a read-only GET of this page on 2026-10-29 was classified "public" (host docs.github.com).

steps.title: Sign in to GitHub and verify the account email
steps.detail: Sign in to the account that will own the app. Users must have a verified email before they can authorize an OAuth app.

steps.title: Register the OAuth app
steps.detail: Open the new-application page and fill in the form. Most fields are free-form; set the Authorization callback URL carefully to a URL you own. The app gets a unique Client ID and Client Secret.
steps.agentPrep: Prepare app name, homepage URL and callback URL values.

steps.title: Store the Client ID and Client Secret securely
steps.detail: Keep them in environment variables or a secret store. The secret is used to exchange the code for an access token; do not leak it from web apps.

steps.title: Implement the authorization flow and choose scopes
steps.detail: Use the web application (authorization code) flow, or the device flow for headless apps; the implicit grant is not supported. Request only the scopes needed for repos, issues, PRs and org access. Add offline_access to opt in to 8-hour tokens with refresh tokens. Cache tokens to avoid hitting the ten-token and sign-in limits.
steps.agentPrep: Draft the scope list and the token refresh/caching logic.

steps.title: Request organization owner approval where restrictions are enabled
steps.detail: When access restrictions are on, members request owner approval for the app and owners are notified of pending requests. Unapproved apps cannot reach private org resources. GitHub's docs do not give a timeline.
steps.agentPrep: Draft the approval request message explaining what the agent reads and why.

steps.title: Test with a real user and org
steps.detail: Authorize with a test account, confirm repo, issue and PR reads, and confirm the app can see (or is blocked from) org resources before and after approval.

scopesAndNuances.text: A token is limited by the user's own access; for example, an admin:org scope does not give admin access if the user is not an org owner.
Source code access cannot currently be scoped to read-only.
Limit of ten tokens per user/application/scope combination and ten tokens created per hour; over the limit, older tokens are revoked or a re-authorization prompt appears.
OAuth apps are limited to 2,000 access token requests per hour, with lower, non-scaling limits compared to GitHub Apps.
API requests made through the app count toward the user's 5,000 requests/hour limit; 15,000/hour applies for members of a GitHub Enterprise Cloud organization that owns or approves the OAuth app.

Access tokens can expire after eight hours with a refresh token that expires after six months without use. Requesting offline_access opts in per sign-in. Existing non-expiring tokens are not changed when expiry is later enforced.

Organizations created new have OAuth app access restrictions on by default; orgs with no restrictions let any OAuth app authorized by a member reach private resources. Privileged OAuth apps can still be authorized.
When an org first sets up restrictions, OAuth apps immediately lose access to its resources and webhook deliveries from private repos stop going to unapproved apps.

blockers.problem: Organization has OAuth app access restrictions and has not approved your app, so private org resources are not accessible.
blockers.fix: Ask the user to request owner approval for the app; org owners get a notification and can approve it.

blockers.problem: Token requests hit rate limits (2,000 token requests/hour; ten tokens per user/app/scope), causing outages or re-authorization prompts.
blockers.fix: Cache and reuse tokens, use refresh tokens, and avoid sign-in loops. Consider a GitHub App for higher, scaling limits.

blockers.problem: The user has not verified their email address, so they cannot authorize the app.
blockers.fix: Have the user verify their email address on GitHub first.
